editorial.title: How to Choose a Web Development Agency in Indonesia: A Practical Checklist
editorial.excerpt: A practical checklist for choosing a web development agency in Indonesia, covering portfolio evidence, process, scope, technology, ownership, QA, security, and support.
keyTakeaways: A web agency should be evaluated against the business outcome, not only the visual quality of homepage screenshots.
A relevant portfolio gives stronger evidence than a generic gallery because it shows whether the team has solved similar content, integration, audience, or technical problems.
A mature process makes assumptions visible early through discovery, information architecture, UX, UI, engineering, QA, launch, and support.
Technology choices should be explainable in terms of requirements, maintainability, integrations, content workflows, performance, security, and future changes.
A proposal should make scope measurable. Vague phrases such as “premium design” are difficult to evaluate without concrete deliverables.
Ownership matters: clarify source code, design files, domains, hosting, analytics, CMS access, documentation, and credentials after launch.

content.text: The practical question in choosing a web development agency at a glance is not whether an option is possible. It is whether it solves the intended business problem with an acceptable level of cost, complexity, risk, and future change. A web agency should be evaluated against the business outcome, not only the visual quality of homepage screenshots.

Teams often make this decision too early. Start by defining the audience, the job the website must perform, and the constraints that could make one approach unsuitable. A relevant portfolio gives stronger evidence than a generic gallery because it shows whether the team has solved similar content, integration, audience, or technical problems.

This is why a visible deliverable can be misleading. Two websites can look similar while having very different content models, integrations, ownership requirements, and operating costs. A mature process makes assumptions visible early through discovery, information architecture, UX, UI, engineering, QA, launch, and support.

A useful evaluation connects the decision to evidence: requirements, user journeys, content needs, technical constraints, and what the team must be able to change after launch. Technology choices should be explainable in terms of requirements, maintainability, integrations, content workflows, performance, security, and future changes.
